question:
Consider the following \(100\) sets of \(10\) elements each:

\[\{1,2,3,\ldots,10\},\] \[\{11,12,13,\ldots,20\},\] \[\{21,22,23,\ldots,30\},\] \[\vdots\] \[\{991,992,993,\ldots,1000\}.\]

How many of these sets contain exactly two multiples of \(7?\)
solution:
Each set contains either one or two multiples of \(7\), so the total number of multiples determines how many sets contain two.

Every seven consecutive integers include a multiple of \(7\), so every ten-number set contains at least one. Three multiples of \(7\) would have their smallest and largest at least \(14\) apart, but a ten-number set has endpoints only \(9\) apart. Thus no set contains three.

There are exactly \(142\) multiples of \(7\) from \(1\) through \(1000\), since
\[
7\cdot142=994\le1000<1001=7\cdot143.
\]
Let \(t\) be the number of sets containing two multiples. The remaining \(100-t\) sets contain one each. These sets partition the integers from \(1\) through \(1000\), so counting the same multiples by set gives
\[
2t+(100-t)=142.
\]
Therefore \(t=\boxed{42}\), choice \(\textbf{B}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Two multiples of \(7\) in one set must be \(7\) apart, so the earlier one must occupy one of the first three positions.

Indeed, three multiples would span at least \(14\), more than the \(9\) between a set's endpoints. Thus any two in a set are consecutive multiples. If the earlier one is in position \(r\), the later one is in position \(r+7\), requiring \(r=1,2,3\). Conversely, a multiple in one of these positions has its next multiple inside the set and its preceding multiple outside.

Because every set begins with a number ending in \(1\), its first three positions have units digits \(1,2,3\). The positive multiples of \(7\) with these endings are respectively
\[
21+70j,\qquad42+70j,\qquad63+70j,
\]
where \(j\) is a nonnegative integer. To justify these lists, the first ten multiples of \(7\) have all ten different units digits; adding \(70\) repeats those endings. Equivalently, two multiples of \(7\) with the same units digit differ by a multiple of both \(7\) and \(10\), hence of \(70\).

For each list, \(j=0,1,\ldots,13\) gives a number at most \(1000\), whereas \(j=14\) exceeds \(1000\). Each list therefore contributes \(14\) earlier multiples. Every qualifying set has exactly one earlier multiple, so none is missed or counted twice.

The total is \(3\cdot14=\boxed{42}\), choice \(\textbf{B}\).
